chunks: And from him, from Ali, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Umar ibn Udhaynah, from Zurarah, who said:
Abdullah ibn Umayr al-Laythi came to Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) and said to him: 'What do you say regarding the mut'ah of women?'
He said: 'Allah has made it permissible in His Book, through the tongue of His Prophet (peace be upon him and his family), so it is halal until the Day of Resurrection.'
He said: 'O Abu Ja'far, one like you says this, while Umar has forbidden it and prohibited it.'
He said: 'Even if he did so.'
He said: 'And I seek refuge in Allah from that, that you make permissible something that Umar has forbidden.'

He said to him: 'Then you are upon the saying of your companion (Umar), and I am upon the saying of the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family). So come, let me challenge you (la'ina) that the true saying is what the Messenger of Allah said, and the falsehood is what your companion said.'
He said: So Abdullah ibn Umayr turned to him and said: 'Does it please you that your wives, your daughters, your sisters, and the daughters of your paternal uncles do that?'
So Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) turned away when he mentioned his wives and the daughters of his paternal un.

key_terms.أُلاَعِنَكَ: I will challenge you (to mutual imprecation)

ai.seo_question: What is the Shia ruling on Mut'ah for women and how does it differ from the view of Umar ibn al-Khattab?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* highlights the theological debate between the Ahl al-Bayt's adherence to the Quranic text and the Sunni reliance on Umar ibn al-Khattab's abrogation (*naskh*) of Mut'ah. Imam al-Baqir (AS) asserts the permanence of the ruling based on divine revelation, challenging the authority of human juristic opinion against prophetic tradition. The narrative concludes with a rhetorical test of consistency, where the Imam's silence upon hearing of his own female relatives practicing it underscores the practical validity of the ruling in early Shia circles.
